ol96b1-aaa555.summary: A sermon-style praeambulum that opens Auriol's Sentences commentary by commending Lombard's work through the theme verse Ezekiel 2:9 ('He spread the book before me, written within and without'). After Gregory's gloss on Scripture as written inwardly (allegory) and outwardly (history), Auriol presents the Sentences as Scripture unrolled and divides the verse into three articles. First, the Master's labor is useful: through the figures of the tabernacle and the fivefold scriptural 'expansion', the Sentences instruct action, support faith, refute heretics, lift the advanced and protect the weak. Second, the book's tenor is easy: it puts proportioned, connected matter before the reader, and through Job 4 the four books are mapped onto God's mysteries, creation, precepts and judgment. Third, the book's worth is admirable: it contains Scripture and treats outward, inward, lower and higher matters (sacraments, grace, sin, Trinity and Incarnation). A prayer to Christ to open the book closes the piece.
claims: The Sentences unfold and make accessible the obscure content of Scripture.
The Sentences serve moral instruction, support of faith, refutation of heresy, aid to the advanced, and protection of the weak.
The four books treat respectively God's mysteries, creation, precepts and virtues, and sacraments and last things.
The Sentences share Scripture's character of being written within and without.

ol96b1-aaa555-d1e104.summary: Title-page rubric of the printed edition, announcing Peter Auriol's questions on the four books of the Sentences and identifying him as cardinal and Friar Minor. It frames the following sermon-style preface; it argues nothing.

ol96b1-aaa555-d1e125.summary: States the theme verse of the principium-style prologue (Ezekiel 2:9): 'He spread the book before me, which was written within and without.' The whole praeambulum unfolds this verse as a commendation of Lombard's Sentences.

ol96b1-aaa555-d1e132.summary: Glosses the theme verse through Gregory the Great. Canonical Scripture is 'rolled up' because it is difficult, and 'written within and without' because of what it is. Gregory's pairs (allegory and history, spiritual and literal sense, invisible promises and visible precepts) give the inner and outer writing, and the outward precepts are plain while the inner mysteries cannot be fully grasped.
claims: Scripture is called rolled up on account of its difficulty.
Scripture is written within by allegory and spiritual sense, and without by history and literal sense.
What Scripture commands outwardly is evident, but what it narrates inwardly cannot be fully apprehended.

ol96b1-aaa555-d1e188.summary: Applies the verse to the Sentences. The book Ezekiel first saw rolled up (2:9) he now sees spread out. So too Scripture, hidden in the canon, is unrolled in Lombard's four books, and every student may say that the Master 'spread the book before me'. Expansion means that what was obscurely said is opened by breadth of understanding.
claims: The Sentences unfold Scripture, which in the canon is hidden from nearly everyone.
To 'expand' the book is to open by understanding what was obscurely stated.

ol96b1-aaa555-d1e225.summary: Divides the theme verse into three points that structure the praeambulum. With respect to the Master it signifies diligent sight, with respect to us a suitable style, and with respect to the book a containing bosom (sinus).
claims: The verse signifies something about the Master, about the readers, and about the book.

ol96b1-aaa555-d1e245.summary: Matches the threefold division to the words of the verse. 'Expandit' shows the Master's diligence, 'coram me' the style fitted to us, and 'liber scriptus intus et foris' the book's capacity. From these the Sentences appear seriously composed (the implicit made explicit), luminously adapted (the hidden presented), and virtuously strengthened (canonical Scripture applied to it).
claims: The Sentences make explicit what Scripture holds implicitly.
The Sentences present hidden truths to the reader.
The Sentences are confirmed by applying canonical Scripture to them.

ol96b1-aaa555-d1e276.summary: Restates the threefold division as the plan of the three articles that follow: the Master's useful labor ('expandit'), the book's easy tenor ('coram me'), and its admirable worth (it contains the book written within and without).

ol96b1-aaa555-d1e287.summary: Rubric introducing the first article of the praeambulum, on the Master's useful labor.

ol96b1-aaa555-d1e292.summary: Opens the first article with a scriptural figure (Exodus 40, the erection of the tabernacle). Like Moses raising the tabernacle with boards, bases, bars, columns and covering, the Master built the Sentences by studious labor.
claims: Lombard composed the Sentences through most studious labor.

ol96b1-aaa555-d1e311.summary: Lists, in rhymed form, five uses of the Sentences: a rudiment for what is to be done, a support for what is to be believed, an argument against the faithless, a help to the advanced, and a protection to the weak.
claims: The Sentences serve five functions: moral instruction, support of faith, refutation of heretics, aid to the advanced, protection of the weak.

ol96b1-aaa555-d1e324.summary: Maps the five functions onto the content of the four books. Lombard instructs about things to be done (especially book 3 on gifts, virtues and precepts), establishes things to be believed (beginning of book 3 and book 4), destroys heretical sayings (throughout), draws out the perfect (especially book 1), and steadies the weak (throughout). The book is thus explanatory, confirmatory, refutative, elevating and guiding.
claims: Book 3 chiefly treats agenda through gifts, virtues and precepts.
Refutation of heretics runs through the whole work.
Book 1 especially serves the advanced.

ol96b1-aaa555-d1e368.summary: Allegorizes the parts of the tabernacle according to the five functions. The boards are the tablets of morals and precepts (rudiment of action), the bases the support of faith, the bars the means of seizing heretics (they are argued against, not armed), the columns the ascent of the advanced, and the covering the protection of the weak. Thus the Master erected the tabernacle of the whole Church.
claims: The Sentences function as the tabernacle of the whole Church.

ol96b1-aaa555-d1e403.summary: Gives a second scriptural figure for the same five functions: the five 'expansions' named in Scripture, of branches, wings, net, light (morning) and cloud. The Master spreads branches to direct action, wings to lift the advanced, a net to catch heretics, light to show the faith, and a cloud to protect the weak. This completes the first article's proof that the Master's labor is useful.
claims: The fivefold scriptural 'expansion' figures the five functions of the Sentences.
The Master's labor in composing the Sentences is useful.

ol96b1-aaa555-d1e466.summary: Rubric introducing the second article, on the book's easy tenor.

ol96b1-aaa555-d1e471.summary: Expounds 'coram me'. Things are 'before us' when proportioned to us as objects, uncovered without a veil, and handed over to us. The Sentences meet all three: they contain matter proportioned to us (unlike the canon), proceed connectedly and therefore clearly, and are handed down to be grasped. The verse of Job 4 then sets up a fourfold mapping: what is above us (book 1, divine mysteries), what was before us (book 2, the beginning of creatures), what was against us as testimony (book 3, precepts), and what will be after us (book 4, the judgment of the dead).
claims: The Sentences treat matters proportioned to human understanding, unlike the scriptural canon.
The Sentences are clear because they proceed connectedly.
Book 1 treats the divine mysteries, book 2 creation, book 3 the precepts, and book 4 the last judgment.

ol96b1-aaa555-d1e539.summary: Applies the first clause of Job 4:13 ('in the horror of a nocturnal vision') to book 1. The divine mystery produces stupor and horror in us, since we see it as by night, that is, obscurely.
claims: The divine mysteries treated in book 1 are seen by us only obscurely.

ol96b1-aaa555-d1e552.summary: Applies the next clauses of Job 4 to books 2 and 3. The beginning of creatures (book 2) matches the 'sleep' that then held people about the truth. The precepts (book 3) produce beauty in the human being, matched to the 'image of a man before my eyes'.
claims: The precepts treated in book 3 produce beauty in the human being.

ol96b1-aaa555-d1e572.summary: Applies the last clause of Job 4 to book 4. The judgment of the dead brings sweetness to those who will hear 'Come, blessed of my Father', the 'voice as of a gentle breeze'. This concludes the second article: the book's tenor is easy because it sets these matters before us.
claims: The last judgment treated in book 4 is sweet for the elect.
The Sentences have an easy tenor because they set these matters before the reader.

ol96b1-aaa555-d1e590.summary: Rubric introducing the third article, on the book's admirable worth.

ol96b1-aaa555-d1e595.summary: Third article: the Sentences contain the book of Scripture and so share its privilege of being written within and without, indeed above, below, within and without, according to their matters. Outwardly apparent are the sacraments and human acts (end of book 3, book 4); inwardly residing are grace and virtues (end of book 2, book 3); downward-dragging are original and actual sin (book 2); upward-raising are the Trinity (book 1) and the Incarnation (book 3). With Apocalypse 5, the book is the sealed book that Christ the Lamb and Lion opened through Peter Lombard's hands. (The opening words are corrupt in the transcription.)
claims: The Sentences contain the content of Scripture and share its quality of being written within and without.
The four books divide their matter into outward, inward, lower and higher subjects.
Christ opened the sealed book of Scripture through Lombard's work.

ol96b1-aaa555-d1e654.summary: Closing prayer of the praeambulum. Undertaking the exposition of this book under God's leadership, we ask Christ, the Lion and Lamb, to open it for us.
